title: Rising early
hookLine: the code asks Sikhs to rise early, bathe and remember

cards: The house is still dark. The street outside hasn't started yet: no buses, no phones buzzing, no one needing anything. Somewhere a tap runs, then stops.
A person sits down on a folded blanket with wet hair and a covered head, and begins the first words of the day under their breath.
The morning prayers have to start somewhere, and the code says where: before the day starts asking. Get up. Wash.

teach.h: AMRIT VELA, THE HOUR BEFORE DAWN.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the code asks a Sikh to wake in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hour before dawn, to bathe, and, with the mind turned toward the one Immortal Being, to repeat the name Waheguru.
The phrase amrit vela isn't new with the code. It comes from Japji Sahib itself, where Guru Nanak says that in the ambrosial hour one should reflect on the true Name and on God's greatness.
And Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, draws a whole day around it.

teach.h: A SIKH OF THE GURU RISES EARLY.
teach.b: In his verse in Gauri, paraphrased: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name; makes the effort in those early hours and bathes; repeats the Name as the Guru teaches; and then, through the day, keeps singing the Guru's word.
Notice where the picture ends. Not at dawn. It runs on into the ordinary hours.
The early quiet is where the day's direction gets set. Now the second verb: bathe.

teach.h: WATER DOESN'T MAKE THE MIND PURE.
teach.b: Japji has a line some readers hear as blunt about what water can't do: cleansing doesn't make the mind pure, even if you wash a hundred thousand times. So the bath isn't the purity. It readies the body.
The remembering is the point. Get up, so you're awake for it. Wash, so you're present in your body for it.

teach.h: THE FIRST WORD GOES TO THE NAME.
teach.b: Then remember, before anything else gets the first word.
The order is the teaching: the first thing the day hears is the Name.

how: Sikhs who keep the code rise in the amrit vela before dawn, bathe, and remember Waheguru before reciting the morning banis; some gurdwaras hold early morning kirtan for those who come.

o: getting up early to finish more work each day
waking before dawn to remember the Name first
a fast kept from sunrise until the evening meal

games.q: the code's morning: tap the pairs.

s: the code asks Sikhs to rise early, bathe and remember the Name
wake in the amrit vela, bathe, and turn the mind to the one Immortal Being.
in Japji, washing is what makes the mind pure
in one reading of Japji's opening, washing doesn't purify the mind, even a hundred thousand times. the remembering is the point.
Guru Ram Das's picture of a Sikh's day ends at dawn
it runs on: through the day, the Sikh keeps singing the Guru's word.

games.q: you're up before dawn, washed, sitting down. what does the Sikh in Guru Ram Das's verse do next?
o: check what the world said overnight.
repeat the Name as the Guru teaches.
plan the whole day's work first.
games.why: the verse says the Sikh repeats the Name as the Guru teaches, and then keeps singing the Guru's word through the day.

practice: Choose a morning this week and rehearse it now: feet on the floor, cold water on your face, sitting down before the phone gets picked up.
Decide what the first word of that day will be, Waheguru said slowly if you pray, or one quiet breath chosen on purpose if not.

wordCard.voice: Rising early. The code's morning: wake in the amrit vela, bathe, and remember the Name before the day begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the ambrosial hour, the time before dawn named in Japji Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: rise and remember. The quiet before the day starts asking. See you in the morning.
